props.title: Nothing's Free
lines: Every return has a price. Volatility is the fee, not a fine.
If you want the return, pay the fee. If you will not pay it, buy a quieter asset.

props.title: Days below the old high are the bill

rows.v: About 11% a year from 1950 to 2019 — with many stretches at least 5% below a previous high.
Netflix returned more than 35,000% from 2002 to 2018, but traded below its previous all-time high on 94% of days.
Monster Beverage returned 319,000% from 1995 to 2018, below its previous high 95% of the time.
A $30,000 car: pay it, buy used, or steal it. Almost nobody chooses steal. In markets, 'steal' is wanting 11% with no drawdowns.
Tickets cost $100. That is the price of the day, not a punishment. Volatility is the same kind of price.
The housing bubble's end cut more than $8 trillion; household wealth fell about $6.2 trillion in the crisis window the book cites.

props.kicker: PAY THE FEE OR BUY LESS RETURN
props.title: Drawdowns are the invoice

rows.v: About 11% a year, 1950–2019, came bundled with long stretches 5% or more below an old high.
More than 35,000% total return, below the old high on 94% of days. The fee was almost every morning.
319,000% from 1995–2018, below the previous high 95% of the time.
Wanting 11% with no drawdowns is the market version of stealing the $30,000 car.
More than $8 trillion of housing wealth and about $6.2 trillion of household wealth gone in the window the book cites — that was a fee, loudly collected.

props.title: Choose the product, then pay
items: If you want equity-like returns, budget for equity-like nausea. Do not call it a bug.
If you will not pay, buy a quieter asset and accept a quieter payoff. That is honest.
